title: Purpura
subject: Medicine
summary: Purpura are non‑blanching skin hemorrhages >5 mm caused by vascular or platelet dysfunction. Recognising patterns, severity and underlying aetiology guides urgent and long‑term management, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Purpura are palpable or non‑palpable red‑purple lesions ≥5 mm that do not fade with pressure, indicating extravasation of blood into the skin.
b: Measure lesion size: petechiae <5 mm, purpura 5–10 mm, ecchymoses >10 mm.
Differentiate from bruises (history of trauma) and vasculitic lesions (tender, raised).

sections.p: Severity is graded by extent, depth and systemic involvement.
b: Mild: limited to skin, no organ dysfunction.
Moderate: skin plus mild abdominal pain or hematuria.
Severe: skin plus renal failure, CNS bleed, or shock.

sections.p: In East African hospitals the commonest causes are infections, immune‑mediated vasculitis and hematologic disorders.
b: Infection‑related: meningococcemia, severe malaria, dengue, viral hemorrhagic fevers.
IgA vasculitis (Henoch‑Schönlein): palpable purpura on legs/buttocks, abdominal pain, hematuria.
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis: asthma, eosinophilia, mononeuritis multiplex, purpura.
Thrombotic microangiopathies: TTP, HUS – thrombocytopenia, MAHA, renal failure.
Drug‑induced: penicillins, sulfonamides, herbal remedies.

sections.p: Patients may present with sudden appearance of red‑purple spots, often symmetric on lower limbs, accompanied by systemic clues.
b: Palpable, tender lesions on legs/buttocks.
Abdominal pain, melena, or vomiting (IgA vasculitis).
Neuropathy or asthma symptoms (EGPA).
Fever, malaise, or rapid deterioration (sepsis, TTP).

t.b: Is there thrombocytopenia or anemia? Low platelets suggest TTP/DIC; normal platelets point to vasculitis.
Are schistocytes present? Indicates microangiopathic hemolysis.
Is there hematuria or proteinuria? Suggests renal involvement (IgA vasculitis, HUS).
Is DIC present? Prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen support sepsis‑related purpura.
Positive MPO‑ANCA supports EGPA; PR3‑ANCA suggests GPA.

b: Rapid fall in platelet count <30 ×10⁹/L.
New neurological deficits or seizures.
Oliguric renal failure or rising creatinine.
Uncontrolled bleeding or shock.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care.
b: Infection: start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) pending cultures.
EGPA: oral prednisolone plus cyclophosphamide for organ‑threatening disease; avoid high‑dose steroids alone if active infection.
TTP: plasma exchange is definitive; if unavailable, give high‑dose methylprednisolone and consider rituximab where feasible.
DIC: treat trigger, give fresh frozen plasma and platelets if bleeding.

sections.p: Monitor organ function and adjust therapy based on response.
b: Weekly platelet count and creatinine until stable.
Educate patients on early signs of bleeding or renal change.
Vaccinate against meningococcus and hepatitis B in at‑risk groups.
Bruising from trauma – usually history of injury, not symmetric, and lesions are not palpable.
Petechial rash of meningococcemia – often accompanied by fever, meningismus, and rapid systemic collapse.
Drug‑induced skin necrosis – tends to be painful, ulcerative, and linked to specific agents.
Normal platelet count does not exclude vasculitis; focus on lesion morphology.
Negative ANCA does not rule out EGPA; eosinophilia and asthma are key.
ADAMTS13 may be normal early in TTP; treat based on clinical pentad.

whenToSeekHelp: New seizures, altered consciousness, or focal neurological signs

faq.q: Can purpura be caused by low platelet count alone?
faq.a: Yes, thrombocytopenia leads to bleeding into the skin, but size and distribution help differentiate from vasculitis.

faq.q: Why is a skin biopsy rarely needed in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Clinical pattern plus basic labs usually identify the cause; biopsy is reserved for atypical or refractory cases.
Avoid high‑dose steroids if an active bacterial infection is suspected, as they can worsen sepsis.

exam: A 7‑year‑old presents with palpable purpura on the legs, colicky abdominal pain and hematuria – what is the most likely diagnosis and next step? — IgA vasculitis; obtain urinalysis and monitor renal function, give supportive care, steroids only if severe.

A patient with asthma, eosinophilia and new mononeuritis multiplex develops purpuric lesions – which vasculitis is suggested and which drug class is first‑line? — EGPA; oral corticosteroids, add cyclophosphamide for organ involvement.

A febrile adult with meningococcal meningitis develops diffuse purpura and a platelet count of 20 ×10⁹/L – what immediate management is required? — Treat meningococcemia with IV ceftriaxone, give platelet transfusion if bleeding, monitor for DIC.

A 45‑year‑old with fever, confusion, thrombocytopenia, anemia and schistocytes on smear – what condition should you suspect and what is the definitive therapy? — TTP; plasma exchange (or plasma infusion if exchange unavailable).
How does the size of a skin lesion help differentiate petechiae from purpura? — Petechiae are <5 mm, purpura 5–10 mm, ecchymoses >10 mm; size reflects depth of bleeding.
Why might a normal ANCA test not exclude EGPA in a low‑resource hospital? — EGPA can be ANCA‑negative; diagnosis relies on asthma, eosinophilia, neuropathy and purpura.
What red‑flag laboratory finding would prompt urgent referral in a child with purpura? — Platelet count <30 ×10⁹/L or rising creatinine indicating renal involvement.

When is a skin biopsy indicated for purpuric rash in a resource‑limited setting? — Only when the clinical picture is atypical, refractory to treatment, or when vasculitis versus coagulopathy cannot be distinguished.
